But finding run/walk success goes well beyond determining your Magic Mile paces, tracking your intervals, and finishing your goal race.
By following some key training principles, you can make your run/walk regimen a fundamental part of your everyday routine. 1. Consistency Is Key
Practice makes perfect, right? Training on a regular basis—even when you’re not working toward a goal race—will help you reach your fitness aims and maintain your run/walk progress.
Now, that doesn’t mean you need to be in race training mode year round. Use one of Runner’s World’s maintenance plans to structure your off-season workouts and sustain your motivation. You can also use our four-week run/walk maintenance plan, which keeps your body prepped before heading into your next training cycle.
2. Prioritize Recovery
All of our run/walk training plans have a weekly rest day for a reason. The time you spend off your feet is when progress happens, allowing your body to soak up all of the hard work you’ve put in. Build in recovery time after your hard workouts and long runs, and also set aside a few minutes each day for recovery methods like stretching or foam rolling.
And don’t forget to catch those z’s! Sleep is one of—if not the—most important recovery tools you can use to your advantage for muscle and tissue repair, improved immune function, and injury prevention, among other benefits.

While it’s important to stay consistent with your running mileage, it’s also important to strength train. We recommend adding strength training into your routine one to three times a week to support stronger muscles, protect your joints, add force behind your stride, and become more resilient.

When choosing a marathon, most runners focus on the details of the race itself: size, location, weather, elevation, and crowd support. Those are crucial considerations, of course, but they only account for one day, compared with the months you spend training for 26.2 miles. So, you also need to factor in what those months of training could look like depending on the race you choose.
Once you do that, you may realize that racing your marathon in the winter or summer actually benefits you more than racing in the spring or fall. In fact, some runners find that the PRs just out of their reach during those more popular racing windows were simply waiting for them in a different season. The missing piece? Moving the timeline of their marathon cycle to maximize factors like consistency.
A run coach who’s competed in every season explains how to pick a race that sets you up to perform at the right time each year and how flipping your training and racing seasons just might lead to more fun, less stress, and even faster times.
Why You Might Not Want to Race in the Fall or Spring
Some of the biggest, most exciting 26.2s occur in the fall and spring—take six of the World Majors, for example. But these marathons can also come with less-than-ideal training timelines, Elizabeth Corkum, a.k.a. Coach Corky, an RRCA-, UESCA-, and USATF-certified run coach, tells Runner’s World.
When race day falls in September, October, or April, you’ll likely have your most important workouts and long runs on tap for the least ideal weather of the summer and winter months: brutal heat and humidity or short days with ice and cold temperatures, Corkum explains. Many runners, though, deem these tougher training conditions a fair trade for a shot at a cool, dry day in the low 50s when they toe the starting line.
Some runners would rather flip the script: Do the bulk of their training and peak mileage weeks in nicer weather, instead of hoping for ideal conditions on race day.
If you don’t enjoy running as much when you’re waking up at 4 a.m. in the summer to beat the heat or waiting until the sun goes down to squeeze in miles just before bed, you may benefit from switching your main training season. Some options to consider might be the California International Marathon (CIM) in December or the Houston Marathon in January, Corkum suggests.
Or, maybe you find yourself worn down from trudging through sleet and slush, bundling up for runs in below-freezing temps, logging miles in the dark when the days shorten, or simply confining yourself to the treadmill because it’s the only place that isn’t slick with ice. In that case, you might want to complete your heaviest training in the spring for a summer race. Some great options to consider are Grandma’s Marathon in June, the San Francisco Marathon in July, and the Gold Coast Marathon in July.
Benefits of Racing in the Summer or Winter
For many runners, the greatest benefit of doing the bulk of their training during the fall and spring is that they enjoy the process more. JPMorgan vs. Bank of America: Which Dividend Stock Is Better for Retirement?
One bank missed earnings after a $1.2 billion settlement charge, while the other just boosted its payout. Yet the cheaper stock with the juicier yield may not be the safer place for retirement income. Three scorecards reveal the tradeoff.

JPMorgan Chase (NYSE:JPM | JPM Price Prediction) or Bank of America (NYSE:BAC): which bank dividend looks stronger for someone building a retirement portfolio right now? Third-quarter earnings made the choice clearer. Bank of America posted adjusted EPS of $1.08, missing the $1.10 estimate, after a $1.2 billion regulatory settlement charge. JPMorgan reported EPS of $5.57 and a 20% return on tangible common equity. In September, it had already raised its quarterly dividend to $1.65 from $1.50.
Both banks make money in the same two ways. The first is net interest income, the gap between what they earn on loans and what they pay on deposits. The second is fees from trading, dealmaking, and wealth management. JPMorgan leans harder on Wall Street: in Q2, corporate and investment bank revenue rose 27% to $24.85 billion. Bank of America runs more like a deposit machine, with $2 trillion in deposits and $1.2 trillion in loans, and its Q3 net interest income rose 8% to $16.45 billion.
Valuation: Bank of America Sells at a Steep Discount
Bank of America trades at 12 times trailing earnings and 10 times forward earnings. JPMorgan trades at 14 times on both measures. On price-to-book, the gap widens to 1.311 versus 2.662. Bank of America shares are down 8.69% year to date, while JPMorgan is up 5.79%. That selloff drives Bank of America’s forward yield to about 2.6% on a $1.28 annualized payout. JPMorgan yields roughly 2.0% on $6.60. Winner: Bank of America.
Dividend Growth and Coverage: JPMorgan Raises Faster
JPMorgan’s quarterly dividend has risen from $1.05 in early 2024 to $1.65, a gain of about 57%. Over the same stretch, Bank of America went from $0.24 to $0.32, about 33%. Coverage is comfortable at both banks. JPMorgan pays out roughly 26% of trailing EPS of $23.84, and Bank of America pays out about 28% of $4.19. CEO Jamie Dimon put the dividend first in line: “After you pay your dividend, which hopefully will be steady, we really like investing in organic growth.” Winner: JPMorgan.
Capital Strength and Risk: JPMorgan Carries the Thicker Cushion
JPMorgan ended Q3 with a CET1 ratio of 13.9%, and Dimon estimates “$30 billion or something of excess capital.” Bank of America’s CET1 ratio is 10.9%, which its CFO describes as 90 basis points above the regulatory minimum. For years, the playbook was simple: athletes focused on their sport first, and financial planning came later. Only after signing a professional contract did they typically hire advisors, accountants and attorneys — and start thinking seriously about managing their wealth.
That timeline often no longer reflects reality. The sports industry has made tremendous strides in creating new ways for athletes to earn money. The next challenge is ensuring they have the knowledge and support to manage it.
Today, many athletes start earning meaningful income long before they turn professional. The College Sports Commission estimates that student-athletes received $1.77 billion in revenue-sharing pay in 2025-2026. Name, Image and Likeness (NIL) opportunities have accelerated that shift, giving student-athletes access to sponsorships and business opportunities while they're still in school.
At the same time, the demand for financial guidance is growing. The 2022 NCAA Student-Athlete Well-Being Study found that many have a strong desire for more resources on financial literacy and taxes.
There is a big focus on creating more earning opportunities for athletes. We now need to put the same energy into helping athletes prepare for the financial responsibilities that come with them.
Decisions are coming earlier
Too often, financial education starts after the money arrives. By then, habits have already formed and important decisions may have already been made.
The reality is that some of the most important financial choices for athletes happen before they sign a major contract. How do taxes work? How much should I save? How do I navigate money conversations with friends and family? Who should I trust?
These aren't professional athlete questions. They're life questions. And athletes are encountering them earlier than ever before.
One thing I've learned from conversations with athletes in my role at J.P. Morgan's Athlete Center of Excellence is that they're eager for this guidance.
I've spoken with current players who — when they were earning NIL income — budgeted for spending and invested the rest, only to find themselves short on cash when tax payments were due. They had the right pieces in place but only became fully engaged when there was a need to be. I've seen a lot of players learn to bring in their financial advisor this way — relying on the advisor to then quarterback communication among their agent, attorney and accountant.
Athletes need to think like CEOs
Athletes should not be expected to be financial experts.
Just as athletes rely on coaches, trainers, nutritionists and medical professionals, they should be able to rely on trusted specialists for financial guidance. But athletes should also have basic financial knowledge so they can ask thoughtful questions, evaluate advice and make informed decisions.
I often encourage athletes to think of themselves as the CEO of their own business. You don't have to master every function of the organization, but you should understand how the pieces fit together and remain engaged in the decisions that affect your future.
That mindset has become increasingly important as athletes build personal brands and create new income streams earlier in their careers. Today's athletes aren't just managing contracts. Many are navigating partnerships, content opportunities, business ventures and NIL deals at a young age.
The financial complexity has increased, and adequate preparation needs to increase with it.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) has already fallen 37% from its recent peak, compared with an average correction of 32% during previous downturns. The bank said indiscriminate selling driven by fears of slowing AI capital expenditure could begin to run its course by early 2027, with congressional policy developments and share repurchases helping restore confidence.
Semiconductor stocks trade at 13.7 times forward earnings, a 22% discount to the S&P 500's 17.7 times multiple. A return to the historical trough valuation of around 12 times earnings would imply at most another 12% downside, according to BofA. The bank also highlighted buyback support from Lam Research, which has a $25 billion programme, ongoing repurchases by Nvidia and Micron's planned buyback start on December 9.
Previous semiconductor downturns suggest the sector typically declines six to nine months ahead of the fundamental earnings turn, before recovering as earnings estimate reductions become reflected in valuations. The SOX has gained an average of 42% during previous recoveries after those cuts were priced in.
BofA sees the late-June 2026 market peak as a potential signal that earnings estimate reductions could begin in the first quarter of 2027, as companies adjust second-half spending plans. However, the bank cautioned that cheaper valuations alone may not be sufficient to restore confidence, with actual earnings cuts likely needed to establish a sustainable floor.
AI spending remains the biggest swing factor
U.S. cloud capital expenditure is currently running at an annualised rate of about $1.2 trillion, with forecasts pointing to more than $1.5 trillion in 2027. If spending stabilises at current levels rather than accelerating, it would represent a roughly 20% downside against 2027 capital expenditure expectations.

A 20% reduction in projected capital expenditure could translate into more than 20% lower sales and a 35% to 40% earnings-per-share headwind for AI-focused semiconductor companies. Nevertheless, BofA said spending reductions could disproportionately affect future land, power and data centre construction, while newer and more efficient chips, including Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform, remain investment priorities.

It might be difficult for some of us, but think about the 1950s for a moment. Specifically, the year 1955. What's significant about that year?
It's the year in which Procter & Gamble (PG -1.02%) started raising its dividend, a streak that remains alive and well today at 71 years. Not only does that make the consumer staples Goliath a Dividend King, or one of the corporations with a payout-increase streak of at least 50 years, it also means the Tide maker is tied for the third-largest dividend-increase streak among U.S. companies.
Think about that. Procter & Gamble's run of consecutive dividend increases is nearly as old as color television, predates the Moon landing by 14 years, and began nearly 20 years before women could get credit cards without a male co-signer. In other words, Procter & Gamble's devotion to steady dividend hikes puts the "long" in "longevity."
Durable in trying economic environments
Call it certainty, consistency, or dependability, but those are very much the reasons why so many investors embrace Dividend Kings, including Procter & Gamble. Market participants certainly love all-weather durability, which the Febreze maker has.
Think about P&G's dividend reliability in the context of recessions. The experts at the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) say there have been 10 official recessions since 1955. Some, such as the COVID-19 economic contraction of 2020, were brief. Others, including the 1981-82 recession and the global financial crisis earlier this century, lasted well over a year.
Through all of that, good times and bad, Procter & Gamble's dividend ticked higher every year. That's the type of dependability that dividend growth investors should prioritize. The consumer defensive label isn't a guarantee against future negative action. Some of the sector's previously storied names have cut payouts.

Choosing between established giants and high-growth disruptors remains a classic dilemma for investors. For those interested in exposure to the tech industry, deciding whether the steady cash generation of Adobe (ADBE -2.90%) or the accelerating momentum of Palantir Technologies (PLTR +3.48%) can be a challenge, as both have different pros and cons.
Adobe provides the software tools for digital creativity, while Palantir focuses on data integration and decision-making software. Both companies are now racing to integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into their core offerings to capture a larger share of enterprise spending.
The case for Adobe
Adobe sells a comprehensive suite of digital tools through various platforms targeting different customer segments. It serves a diverse audience, including professional designers, students, and large global enterprises that rely on its proprietary formats. The company has integrated its Firefly generative artificial intelligence models directly into its software, helping users create content more efficiently.
In its 2025 fiscal year (FY), ended last Nov. 28, revenue reached $23.8 billion, representing a revenue growth of 10.5% compared to the previous year. The company reported a net income of $7.1 billion, which reflects a healthy net margin of 30%. This growth is supported by a sticky subscription model that provides predictable recurring revenue from its massive base of over one billion monthly active users.
As of its November 2025 balance sheet, Adobe maintains a stable financial position with a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.6x. This ratio compares total debt to shareholder equity to measure financial leverage. The current ratio, which measures the ability to pay short-term obligations with short-term assets, stands at 1.0x. During the same period, the company generated $9.9 billion in free cash flow, providing significant capital for reinvestment or acquisitions.
The case for Palantir Technologies
Palantir Technologies builds sophisticated software solutions, such as its artificial intelligence platform (AIP), that help organizations analyze complex data. Its strategy involves securing long-term contracts with government agencies and expanding rapidly into the commercial sector with partnerships like Amerilife and Changshin. The company positions AIP as a central operating system that allows businesses to deploy large language models (LLMs) safely and effectively.
In FY 2025, ended Dec. 31, revenue reached $4.5 billion, marking a significant revenue growth of 56.2% over the prior year. This acceleration helped the company achieve a net income of $1.6 billion, resulting in a net margin of 36.3%. The rapid expansion in the commercial segment has become a primary driver of overall growth, as more businesses seek to modernize their data operations.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, Palantir Technologies carries a debt-to-equity ratio of zero, indicating it has very little debt relative to its equity. Its current ratio is 7.1x, which suggests a very high level of liquidity for its daily operations. The company generated $2.1 billion in free cash flow in FY 2025. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented roughly 32% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Key Takeaways
- Qualcomm rose 5.5% Friday after Alphabet disclosed a $548 million stake, days after weak handset sales hit the stock following earnings.
- Handset revenue fell 26% to $5.14 billion, while automotive revenue jumped 89% to a record $1.99 billion.
- CEO Cristiano Amon expects handset units to stay flat to down in calendar 2027, putting the burden on data centers and cars.
- The February 3 report, guided to $10.4 billion to $11.2 billion of revenue, is the next test.
Qualcomm (QCOM) got a vote of confidence from a new data center partner on Friday.
Alphabet (GOOGL) disclosed a $548 million stake in the chipmaker, and the shares rose 5.5% to $165. It came days after Qualcomm announced a multi-generational product collaboration with Amazon (AMZN) for AI data centers.
The bounce followed a rough week. Qualcomm slumped after its November 4 report as weak smartphone chip sales overshadowed data center momentum, and the broad chip selloff on November 5 piled on.
Even after Friday, the stock is down 13% over six months and 36% below its $260 52-week high.
Handsets fell, cars took off
The quarter split cleanly in two.
- Non-GAAP EPS of $2.17 edged past the $2.16 estimate but fell 28% from $3.00.
- Handset revenue dropped 26% to $5.14 billion.
- Automotive revenue rose 89% to a record $1.99 billion, its first quarter near $2 billion.
GAAP revenue fell 8% to $10.32 billion. Restructuring charges, mostly severance, pulled GAAP EPS down to $1.17.
Total revenue shows how much handsets still dominate…
Revenue has now fallen year over year for consecutive quarters, so cars and data centers have a big hole to fill.
Betting on non-handset growth
Amon says the turn starts now. “Fiscal 2027 marks the start of our non-handset revenue inflection, including the ramp of our Data Center business,” he said in the earnings release.
Management projects non-handset revenue to grow more than 60% in fiscal 2027 and reiterated a $5 billion data center revenue target for the year. Qualcomm also renewed long-term licensing deals with Apple, Huawei and Transsion, which steadies the royalty side.
Alphabet’s stake is a signal more than a financial event. At $548 million, it equals about 0.3% of Qualcomm’s $177 billion market value.
Handsets will keep hurting. Amon said on the call that the plan assumes global handset units will remain flat to down in calendar 2027.
Can consensus growth survive that?
Analysts expect about 10% annual revenue growth over the next two years. That forecast leans heavily on the data center ramp showing up on time.

P&G's dividend has risen more than 60% over the past decade, and if the next 10 years look like the last 10, that $260-ish becomes something north of $430 a year on the same shares, without buying another one. The point of owning P&G is not the yield you get today. It is the yield you get on the price you paid, 10 and 20 years from now, from a company that has never once broken the streak.

Households squeezed by high grocery and gas prices are facing another hit: rising costs for home repairs and upgrades.
The cost of repairing or remodeling a home has risen steadily through October, with higher oil and energy prices, along with elevated interest rates stemming from the Iran conflict, pushing prices up. In the three months through June, it rose at the fastest quarterly pace since October 2024, according to insurance data analytics provider Verisk.
Repair bills could climb further as manufacturers of paint, plumbing fixtures, appliances and air conditioners — which already lifted prices last year due to tariffs — push through another round of increases to offset higher materials and freight costs.
“Just to put it in perspective, this quarter was the most significant inflationary period that we’ve experienced since mid-2022,” Armstrong World Industries Inc. Chief Executive Officer Mark Hershey said on an earnings call. The ceiling maker raised prices in November, noting its freight costs had risen about 20% from a year earlier.
Paint producer Sherwin-Williams Co. raised prices 8% in September and hasn’t ruled out further hikes. Pool Corp. did the same, as did HVAC manufacturer Carrier Global Corp., citing higher steel, copper, aluminum and freight costs, expecting inflationary pressures to persist into 2027.
Whirlpool Corp., which sells the KitchenAid, Maytag and inSinkErator labels alongside its namesake brand, will boost US prices by 7% in December.
“We will have meaningful inflation to address in 2027,” construction tools make Stanley Black & Decker Inc. Chief Financial Officer Patrick Hallinan said on an earnings call. “We plan to do so with productivity measures and pricing actions, with a price increase likely around the turn of the year.”
The ability to pass along higher costs to consumers depends on the product, said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Drew Reading. Homeowners are less able to avoid repairs and maintenance, though they may trade down on items like faucets or toilets.
That silver lining may put a floor under earnings. Roofing maker Carlisle Cos Inc. expects current pricing to become a tailwind as costs normalize in 2027. Price increases are expected to catch up with rising costs by the end of 2026. So far, higher prices have not hurt demand or prompted more pre-buying, CEO Christian Koch said in an earnings call.
Masco Corp., which makes faucets under brands including Hansgrohe, credited pricing with partly helping drive a 13% adjusted operating profit increase in the third quarter. Regarding potential price hikes in 2027, CEO Jonathon Nudi said pricing is the “last lever we pull.”
Existing price increases largely reflect earlier tariff and input-cost mitigation, Reading said. Accelerating copper, oil-based materials and freight costs create the potential need for Masco to raise prices in 2027.
That adds to a long-running squeeze on homeowners, with repair and remodeling costs already at a decade high, up about 64% since 2016 as of October, Verisk data shows.
Further increases are more likely to weaken demand for big-ticket discretionary items, Reading said.
Some households are already putting off larger purchases and repairing appliances rather than replacing them, according to Whirlpool CEO Marc Bitzer, though “at one point, people will replace it.”

If your home isn’t in a federally designated flood zone, flooding might seem like someone else’s problem. No one requires you to buy flood insurance, and the map suggests you’re in the clear. But reality may be very different.
Mounting evidence reveals that significantly more homes are at risk of flooding than is indicated by FEMA’s 100-year flood maps – about 6 million more, and 14.6 million properties in all, by one estimate. The official maps are commonly outdated, and some are two decades old. Even when updated, they typically rely on historical flood data rather than future risk projections.
But there’s another problem that redrawing the lines won’t solve.
FEMA’s flood maps answer only one question: Is the water likely to reach my neighborhood? They don’t assess an individual home’s risks or what the impacts are likely to be when the water rises.
To understand the impact, more comprehensive data is needed, including the probable flood depth at the home, the building’s age and construction quality, and insurance coverage.
Same street, different risks
When these other factors are considered, your home’s true flood risk is far more complex than the map might seem to indicate.
The data shows how two houses on the same street can face radically different risks from flooding, even when located in the same flood zone – and where local governments can help.
One home may be newer, well maintained and covered by flood insurance. Another may be decades older, at the low end of the same street where water runs deeper during a flood, and is in poor repair and uninsured. The same storm would leave them in very different predicaments, with very different paths to recovery.
Neighborhood averages can make it hard to tell which homes are likely to be hit hardest. But understanding an individual property’s risks matters for residents figuring out how to protect a home, and for local officials deciding where limited flood-protection money should go.
We study how flooding affects homes and the people who live in them. To see how much these house-by-house differences matter, we and colleagues Aaron Flores of Arizona State University and Sara Meerow of the University of Colorado Boulder built a detailed flood risk score for nearly 1 million homes in Houston. We describe the results in a new study published in the journal Applied Geography.
Our past research in Houston found that more than half of 100,000 documented flood-prone buildings in the city currently lie outside official flood boundaries, and that these overlooked buildings are more likely to be in poor condition and uninsured, leaving them especially exposed when the floodwaters do come.
The new research helps communities locate those homes.

– Water: How deep would floodwaters likely get at the home in a 100-year flood event, defined as having a 1% chance of occurrence in any given year? Asphalt-roofing manufacturers have come out swinging against a new Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety standard that limits the coveted “Fortified” designation to roofs younger than 15 years. The manufacturers’ response could lend new fuel to the debate over whether insurers can or should refuse to write some aging roof systems.
The IBHS’ “sweeping conclusions are fundamentally compromised by non-standard testing protocols, unrepresentative grab-sampling, and incomplete probabilistic modeling,” the Asphalt Roofing Manufacturers Association said in recent news release. “By shifting testing procedures mid-project and omitting positive performance outcomes along with enhanced manufacturer installation guidelines, the study fails to reflect real-world roof system durability.”
The IBHS report and a technical bulletin released in September looked at IBHS’ 10-year-long study of shingles at its roof farms around the country, as well as roof examinations after three windstorm events in recent years.
The pushback over the reports comes as the Fortified designation has become the gold standard for homes built to resist high winds, with more states adopting the standard through grant-funded wind-mitigation programs or similar building codes. The IBHS, funded by the property/casualty insurance industry, reported in May that more than 100,000 structures have been designated as Fortified, with Alabama leading the way with more than half of the Fortified homes in the country. That’s double the number from 2023.
The Institute’s Sept. 29 Fortified bulletin notes that homes with roofs more than 15 years old cannot continue to win the Fortified roof designation, a certification that can lead to significant premium discounts from property insurers. The rule takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.
Institute officials could not be reached for comment, but the IBHS bulletin emphasized that the requirement applies only to Fortified home re-certification. “It does not establish asphalt shingle service life, determine whether an individual roof is fit for continued use or requires roof replacement at a particular age for any purpose other than FORTIFIED eligibility,” the bulletin reads.
Still, roofing companies worry that the IBHS reports paint too broad a brush stroke and could prompt insurers to adopt similar restrictions on any type of shingle roof, just as several Florida-based carriers did in recent years. Some of those insurers in the early 2000s—during the height of the claims litigation and assignment-of-benefits crisis in Florida—began dropping coverage for Florida homes with roofs that were older than 10 years, despite roof manufacturers’ warranties that the shingles were built to last as much as 30 years in some cases.

Only a handful of other states, including Texas and Virginia, have adopted similar governance on insurers’ renewals based solely on roof age, according to news reports and the Texas Department of Insurance.

A fire barreled through a multifamily row house in New York early Thursday, killing six people and injuring nine others, including some firefighters and police officers, the city’s fire department said.
More than 200 first responders descended on the two-story building in Brooklyn’s Sunset Park neighborhood, where Kevin Woods, the department’s chief of fire operations, said they were met with “fire on every floor.”
The severely charred building had “fire blowing out every window, meeting us at the front door,” he said at a news conference. Fire marshals were still investigating what caused the blaze.
Firefighters rescued four people, using a rear entrance to reach people trapped behind window bars, Woods said. A staircase partially collapsed inside the building, he added.
First responders brought the fire under control in about three hours, and eight people who were displaced were taken to hotels. Woods said the fire spread to one adjacent row house, but damage could be seen on buildings to both its left and right.
Row houses share common walls and exteriors and are usually built in blocks. Fire officials said the building was part of a block of 25 wood-frame homes in Sunset Park, a densely populated working-class neighborhood in southwestern Brooklyn with large Asian and Hispanic populations.
“This was a devastating fire,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at the news conference. “It will take a long time for this neighborhood to mourn the neighbors they lost this morning and to recover from this immense grief.”
The nine injured people were expected to survive, including three firefighters and two police officers who had minor injuries. No names have been released.
A lithium-ion battery was found at the scene, but it was unknown whether it was related to the fire, the department said.
Last week, an e-bike battery fire killed four people in the Bronx. It is among more than 400 fires in the city that have been linked to lithium-ion batteries this year, leading to at least six deaths and more than 70 injuries, fire officials said.
Property records show that the Brooklyn row house was erected in 1915. A family sold it a few years ago to a company called One Golden Sunshine Corp., according to city records.
Complaints filed with the city’s Department of Buildings in 2025 alleged that the basement level was illegally being converted into an apartment, and construction was underway without permits. The two apartments on the first and second floors also had been illegally divided into three units, the complaints alleged.
City inspectors visited several times — most recently in August — but were unable to gain access, according to department records. It is standard protocol to close a complaint after multiple unsuccessful entry attempts, according to a 2025 city audit of the department’s enforcement actions.
Building inspectors do not have legal authority to force entry, though they can seek a warrant depending on the severity of the complaint.

The spirit of the fall marathon is undeniably contagious: the roaring crowds, the crisp autumn air, and massive community energy. If you spectated this year, watching the hundreds (if not thousands) of runners race toward the finish line might have you yearning to lace up your shoes and hit the starting line next season. But before you jump into training, hit pause and make sure you’re prepared for success.
“Training to run a marathon will revolutionize your life, but it will also test you in brand-new ways,” says Susie Crossland-Dwyer, an avid marathoner and ultramarathoner, coach, and founder of studio s in Cincinnati. “A lot goes into a healthy, successful training season and what you do leading up to it.”
Here are nine tips that coaches want every marathoner to know to get to race day healthy, strong, and fast!
1. Make Sure You Have an Adequate Base
You’re about to set out on four-plus months of intense weekly mileage. That’s really tough on your body. To sidestep an overuse injury, having a steady foundation is crucial. A review of research on runners’ injuries published in the Journal of Sport and Health Science found that the injury incidence rate among runners is 40.2 percent, and overuse from ramping up mileage or intensity too quickly causes more than 70 percent of the injuries.
“As you begin your marathon season, start with base building and don’t just jump right into doing all the miles and all the speed workouts,” advises Crossland-Dwyer, who recommends spending at least three months gradually working up to 20 to 25 miles per week before starting an official marathon training program.
2. Start Resistance Workouts
“Strength training, specifically your core and hips, is the most effective way to prevent injuries,” says Jeff Gaudette, owner and head coach at RunnersConnect. “As you ramp up your mileage for the marathon, this will be essential to you staying healthy through the training segment.”
Studies have found that strength training can also boost your performance by improving your running economy. You don’t need a certain base of strength before starting your training plan, he says, but you should include two to three weight workouts each week.
Along with weight training, “try plyometrics to get your body used to absorbing impact, single-leg exercises to prevent muscle imbalances, and mobility drills to keep your range of motion and joints healthy,” advises Meg Takacs, NASM-CPT, a run coach and founder of the Movement & Miles app.
3. Figure Out a Fueling Plan
Carb-loading before race day is what most novice runners are familiar with when starting on their marathon-training journey, but it’s only one aspect of your diet that’s important.
“Nutrition is key for successful training and a successful race—from carbs to water, electrolytes, and salt capsules,” says Takacs. “The goal is to stay ahead of any deficits before they happen because once you’re in a hydration or nutritional deficit, it’s almost impossible to come back.”
Buy water bottles to carry with you on long runs (sip water or a sports drink every 10 to 15 minutes), plus gels or gummies to nibble on every 30 minutes to stay fueled and strong through your long runs ahead.
4. Be Realistic About Training Time
We’re not talking about the race itself—though, yes, you’re going to be on your feet for a long time for that, too. But it’s important to know the kind of time commitment you’re going to be looking at for the next 16 or so weeks leading up to race day.

Permits are the new bottleneck

Texas is the flashpoint: Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on a moratorium on new data centers, and Wells Fargo puts 27% of planned US data center gigawatts in the state. SpaceX already had about 2.2 gigawatts of compute running at the end of October. Applied Digital, though, still has most of its build ahead of it. Its leases cover 1.41 GW, worth about $36 billion over their base terms, but only 250 MW was live at the start of October. Days after voters ousted all three Republican justices on the 15th Court of Appeals in Tuesday’s election, the court canceled oral arguments for four cases, telling lawyers the case will be reset “at a later date.”
The change will leave the cases — including a challenge to state rules limiting the sale of hemp-derived products containing THC — to three Democrats who will take office in early January.
The THC regulations, originally set to take effect at the end of March, included child-resistant packaging, a significant increase in licensing fees, new labeling, testing and bookkeeping requirements. The Texas Department of State Health Services rules also codified the legal purchasing age to 21 and increased licensing fees for manufacturers of hemp-derived THC from $258 to $10,000 per facility and retail registrations from $155 to $5,000. Industry leaders said the fees amounted to a ban by forcing businesses to close.
Smoke shops briefly pulled the products from shelves as the ban went into effect before a Travis County district judge on April 10 temporarily blocked the rules as a lawsuit by the hemp industry played out in court.
The 15th Court of Appeals, which has statewide jurisdiction over challenges to state laws and regulations, was set to hear oral arguments in the case Dec. 8.
The cancellation will let current justices deliver opinions on already argued cases, Justice Scott Field told Bloomberg Law.
“We know we can’t get the opinion out for cases orally argued before the end of the year so we don’t want to waste the lawyers’ time with an argument if there’s a chance the new court will also want to hear argument,” Field said.
There are 39 cases before the outgoing justices that have already presented oral or written arguments and are awaiting opinions.
Oral arguments set for Dec. 8 and 9 also were canceled in:
• The State of Texas vs. Sunrise Community Church Inc., a legal battle around a homeless shelter in South Austin. The attorney general’s office argued the shelter’s proximity to an elementary school makes it a public nuisance.
• Comptroller Don Huffines and Attorney General Ken Paxton vs. City of Lancaster, a dispute over about $3 million in sales taxes.
• Huffines and Paxton vs. Dave & Buster’s, which sued to recover $2.58 million that the company believed qualified for tax exemptions.

P&G challenged claims that Dove Deep Moisture Body Wash provides moisturizing benefits for 24 hours after use, including "Nourishes Deeply for 24-Hours," "24HR renewing MicroMoisture," and "round-the-clock deep moisture." P&G also challenged claims that the product nourishes the driest skin, as well as the product name "Deep Moisture."
The 24-Hour Claims
Unilever supported its 24-hour moisturization claims with a short-term moisturization study (STM Study) designed to measure skin hydration over 24 hours following a single wash with Dove Deep Moisture Body Wash. NAD found that Unilever's STM Study is an appropriate study to measure moisture on the skin. P&G submitted studies challenging the STM Study, but NAD concluded that P&G had not shown Unilever's STM Study was flawed or that its own studies were more reliable. NAD therefore found Unilever's evidence sufficient to support its claims that Dove Deep Moisture Body Wash moisturizes skin for 24 hours and provides continued moisture renewal and regeneration.
The "Round-the-Clock" Claim
P&G also challenged the "round-the-clock deep moisture" claim, arguing that it conveys significant moisturizing benefits for an extended period after in-shower use. NAD found that, because the claim appears above language stating that the product "restores moisture for 24 hours," consumers could reasonably understand it to promise 24-hour moisturization. Having found the 24-hour claims supported, NAD determined that the round-the-clock claim was also supported.
The Nourishes Claim
P&G challenged the claim that Dove Deep Moisture Body Wash "NOURISHES THE DRIEST SKIN" and "actively regenerates skin's natural moisture." Unilever cited deposition studies showing that the body wash deposits fatty acids on and within the skin's outer layer, helping restore lipids that support the skin barrier and moisture retention.

Capstone will operate as a dedicated IP&E business while retaining access to Arrow’s existing semiconductor, engineering, digital and supply chain capabilities.

Arrow plans to introduce Capstone at the electronica trade show in Munich, Germany, scheduled for November 10–13, 2026.
A standalone Capstone website is expected to launch during the first quarter of 2027, enabling customers to source IP&E products directly through the new platform.
Until the website becomes operational, customers will continue to access Arrow’s IP&E portfolio through its existing website and sales channels.
Capstone will remain integrated with Arrow’s broader technical and commercial resources despite operating as a separate business unit.
